title: Research
text:
This project examines equity in FEMA Individual Assistance using Hurricane Harvey as an empirical case.
The study combines FEMA Individual Assistance records with socioeconomic and spatial data, including measures of disaster exposure such as rainfall intensity. FEMA administrative records reflect household applications and agency determinations of assistance eligibility and awards, while the additional socioeconomic and spatial data characterize the communities and disaster conditions in which those assistance decisions occurred.

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends
text:
Results
The website CSV covered September 1, 2021, through September 1, 2026, with monthly observations. Changing the window to the past year produced weekly observations. Google Trends reports relative search interest rather than search counts: 100 represents the peak within a query, while 0 may indicate insufficient search volume rather than no searches. Removing Election changed the values of the remaining terms because Google rescaled the comparison.
The website and R results were not identical. The website returned 61 monthly observations, while R returned 262 weekly observations. The peak value for Trump was 40 on the website and 25 in R, whereas Election reached 100 in both. A direct date-by-date comparison was not appropriate because the intervals differed. In addition, the website searched Kamala Harris, while the provided R script searched the broader term Harris.

library(gtrendsR)

TrumpHarrisElection = gtrends(
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

the_df = TrumpHarrisElection$interest_over_time
plot(TrumpHarrisElection)

title: Assignment 2: Google Trends
text:
Comparison of the Two Methods
The website requires the researcher to record query parameters manually, whereas the R object records parameters such as the keyword, geography, time window, search type, and category. R is easier to reproduce and scale to many searches, although large collections require multiple queries and careful normalization. Both methods rely on sampled and rescaled Google Trends data. The website interface can change, while gtrendsR can fail because of rate limits or changes to the service; caching successful pulls helps preserve provenance and detect problems.
The R object also contained country, region, DMA, city, related-topic, and related-query data that were absent from the website CSV. Harris and Kamala Harris produced different series because the broader term can represent other people, places, and organizations. Two R pulls conducted approximately ten minutes apart were identical in this instance, but sampled Trends results are not guaranteed to remain identical in future pulls.

title: Assignment 3
text:
Uncertainty Check
Dimmit County has an estimated poverty rate of 41.1% with a margin of error of 8.9 percentage points, producing an approximate 90% confidence interval of 32.2% to 50.0%. Zapata County has an estimated poverty rate of 38.4% with a margin of error of 6.0 percentage points, producing an interval of 32.4% to 44.4%. Because these intervals overlap substantially, the published ranking does not demonstrate that Dimmit County’s true poverty rate is higher than Zapata County’s. The ordering should therefore be interpreted as a ranking of point estimates rather than a definitive difference between the counties.

title: Assignment 3
text:
Methods Note
This analysis uses the 2024 ACS 5-year estimates for all 254 counties in Texas. County geography was selected because it provides meaningful comparisons across the state while remaining readable on a single map. Median household income (B19013_001) is mapped to show the spatial distribution of economic resources. Poverty status (B17001_002) and its corresponding universe (B17001_001) are used to calculate county poverty rates rather than raw counts, which would largely reflect differences in population size.
The poverty-rate margin of error was calculated with moe_prop() using the margins of error for both the numerator and denominator. The estimates show substantial geographic variation, but several counties—particularly those with small populations—have wide margins of error. Therefore, the top and bottom rankings should be interpreted cautiously. Overlapping confidence intervals indicate that small differences in the point estimates do not necessarily represent meaningful differences in the underlying county poverty rates.

title: Assignment 5: Government Data API
text:
I downloaded ten hearings of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations using two methods: links from a CSV exported from the GovInfo search page and results obtained through the GovInfo API. On the website, I searched for Senate Committee on Foreign Relations hearings, applied the Senate Foreign Relations Committee filter, and sorted the results newest first.
The initial API query, collection:(CHRG) AND "Committee on Foreign Relations", produced a different list: only six of the ten documents matched the website results. Changing the keywords alone did not resolve the difference. I then used collection:CHRG AND chamber:senate AND committee:"Foreign Relations" and sorted by publication date in descending order. The revised API results matched all ten website document IDs in the same order. Both methods successfully downloaded all ten PDFs, and I saved separate download logs.

On the website, I searched for Senate Committee on Foreign Relations hearings, applied the Senate Foreign Relations Committee filter, and sorted the results newest first.
The initial API query, collection:(CHRG) AND "Committee on Foreign Relations", produced a different list: only six of the ten documents matched the website results. Changing the keywords alone did not resolve the difference. I then used collection:CHRG AND chamber:senate AND committee:"Foreign Relations" and sorted by publication date in descending order. The revised API results matched all ten website document IDs in the same order. Both methods successfully downloaded all ten PDFs, and I saved separate download logs.

title: Assignment 5: Government Data API
text:
Difficulties Encountered
First, the example CSV code used skip = 2, which skipped the header and the first document in my export. As a result, a document row was incorrectly treated as column names. Removing this argument fixed the problem.
Second, the initial API downloads failed because the PDF requests did not include the API key. Adding the key to each download request resolved the failures. The code retrieved the key from the environment rather than including it directly in the script.
Finally, the initial search mismatch showed that a phrase appearing in document text is not equivalent to filtering by committee metadata. Explicitly specifying the collection, chamber, and committee produced the intended results.

title: Assignment 5: Government Data API
section: Usability of the Documents as Data
text:
Usability of the Documents as Data
I used pdftools::pdf_text() to test text extraction from all ten PDFs. The documents ranged from 31 to 63 pages, and text was extracted from every document. Each PDF contained one page with no extracted text; I did not verify whether these were genuinely blank pages. The extraction also produced repeated ligature-parsing error messages. The first document’s cover and a middle-page sample were readable, but this limited inspection does not establish that all extracted text is accurate.
To create a document-level table, I could use one row per hearing and columns for its document ID, title, date, page count, and download status. Creating a table of speakers and statements would require additional parsing of the transcript.
To create a corpus, the extracted text would need cleaning. The sample retained page numbers, extra spaces, line breaks, and words split across lines, such as engage- followed by ments. I would remove repeated headers and page numbers, normalize whitespace, and carefully reconnect words broken at line endings. Document IDs and page references should be retained, and a speaker-level corpus would also require identifying speaker labels and separating their statements.

title: Assignment 5: Government Data API
text:
Improvements to the Process
I would use explicit metadata filters from the beginning and compare document IDs before downloading. I would also read the export’s header before applying any row-skipping settings and include authentication in every API download request.
For text analysis, I would test the available HTML/text versions and compare samples with the PDFs to determine whether they reduce extraction problems. Metadata provides document IDs, titles, dates, and download links without opening each PDF, allowing a document inventory to be created before processing the transcripts. Download logs should record successes and failures so unsuccessful requests can be identified and retried.

title: Assignment 5: Government Data API
text:
What the API Added
The API allowed me to express the search, filters, and sorting in code and repeat the collection process without manually exporting a new results list. Compared with scraping webpage markup, it returned structured metadata and download links without requiring me to parse the webpage layout.

title: Assignment 4: Web Scraping and Data Acquisition Plan
text:
1. Books to Scrape
I extracted each book’s title, displayed price, and rating from the first five catalog pages. I also converted the price to a numeric variable while retaining the original text. The five pages produced 100 records, with 20 books per page and no missing values in the requested fields.


Code
scrape_books <- function(page_number) {
  url <- paste0(
    "https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-",
    page_number,
    ".html"
  )

  page <- read_html(url)

  result <- tibble(
    page = page_number,
    title = page |>
      html_elements("article.product_pod h3 a") |>
      html_attr("title"),
    price = page |>
      html_elements("article.product_pod p.price_color") |>
      html_text2(),
    rating = page |>
      html_elements("article.product_pod p.star-rating") |>
      html_attr("class") |>
      str_remove("star-rating ")
  ) |>
    mutate(price_gbp = parse_number(price))

  Sys.sleep(1)
  result
}

books <- bind_rows(lapply(1:5, scrape_books))

title: Assignment 4: Web Scraping and Data Acquisition Plan
text:
2. Wikipedia tables

Foreign-exchange reserves
I first inspected all tables with the wikitable class instead of assuming that the first table had the needed structure. The page contained two candidate tables. The first was the country-level reserves table, with 198 rows and 8 columns before cleaning.
The table required more cleaning than its displayed appearance suggested. The first two rows were a multi-row header, and four columns shared the same name. I assigned meaningful column names, removed the two header rows, and selected the including gold, US$ million column. I then removed reference markers, normalized nonbreaking and thin spaces, excluded any Total or World row, and converted the reserve amount to a number. Dates appeared with both full and abbreviated month names, so I extracted the day, month, and year rather than relying on one date format. The final file contains 196 countries or areas. Albania’s source value was 31 Apr 2024, which is not a valid date, so I retained the original text and left the parsed date missing rather than changing it.


Code
wiki_url <- paste0(
  "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/",
  "List_of_countries_by_foreign-exchange_reserves"
)

wiki_page <- read_html(wiki_url)
tables <- wiki_page |> html_elements("table.wikitable")

lapply(tables |> html_table(), dim)
reserves_raw <- tables[[1]] |> html_table()

names(reserves_raw) <- c(
  "country", "continent", "reserve_1", "reserve_2",
  "reserve_3", "reserve_4", "date", "reference"
)

reserves <- reserves_raw |>
  slice(-(1:2)) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.character),
      ~ .x |>
        str_remove_all("\\[.*?\\]") |>
        str_replace_all("[\\u00A0\\u2009\\u202F]", " ") |>
        str_squish()
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!str_detect(country, regex("total|world", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  transmute(
    country,
    continent,
    reserves_million_usd = parse_number(str_remove_all(reserve_1, " ")),
    date_original = date
  )

parse_wiki_date <- function(x) {
  parts <- str_match(
    x,
    "^(\\d{1,2})\\s+([[:alpha:]]+)\\s+(\\d{4})$"
  )
  month_number <- match(
    str_to_title(str_sub(parts[, 3], 1, 3)),
    month.abb
  )
  parse_date(
    sprintf(
      "%s-%02d-%02d",
      parts[, 4], month_number, as.integer(parts[, 2])
    )
  )
}

reserves <- reserves |>
  mutate(reported_date = parse_wiki_date(date_original))

A different target: population
For the second target, I used Wikipedia’s table of countries and dependencies by population. The raw table contained 240 rows and 6 columns. Changing the target showed why a Wikipedia scraper cannot assume a stable schema. This table had different column names, only one candidate table, and no extra header rows. Its World row was an actual summary record rather than part of a multi-row header. It also mixed complete dates with year-only values. Therefore, the column-renaming, row-removal, and date-parsing rules from the reserves table could not be reused without modification.
After removing the World row, footnote markers, and unnecessary columns, I converted population to a number and preserved the original date text. For 229 rows, a complete date could be parsed. Ten rows reported only a year; I recorded the year and labeled the precision as year only instead of inventing a month and day. The cleaned table contains 239 rows and no missing population or reported-year values.


Code
population_url <- paste0(
  "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/",
  "List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population"
)

population_raw <- population_url |>
  read_html() |>
  html_elements("table.wikitable") |>
  html_table() |>
  .[[1]]

names(population_raw) <- c(
  "country", "population", "world_share",
  "date", "source", "notes"
)

population <- population_raw |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.character),
      ~ .x |>
        str_remove_all("\\[.*?\\]") |>
        str_replace_all("[\\u00A0\\u2009\\u202F]", " ") |>
        str_squish()
    )
  ) |>
  filter(country != "World") |>
  transmute(
    country,
    population = parse_number(str_remove_all(population, " ")),
    date_original = date,
    source
  ) |>
  mutate(
    reported_year = parse_integer(str_extract(date_original, "\\d{4}$")),
    reported_date = if_else(
      str_detect(date_original, "^\\d{4}$"),
      as.Date(NA),
      parse_wiki_date(date_original)
    ),
    date_precision = if_else(
      str_detect(date_original, "^\\d{4}$"),
      "year only",
      "full date"
    )
  )

title: Assignment 4: Web Scraping and Data Acquisition Plan
section: 3. Comparison with the World Bank API
text:
3. Comparison with the World Bank API
I retrieved the World Bank indicator FI.RES.TOTL.CD, Total reserves (includes gold, current US$), with one WDI() call. I requested 2015–2024, removed aggregate regions, and divided the values by one million so the unit matched the Wikipedia table.


Code
library(WDI)

reserves_api <- WDI(
  indicator = "FI.RES.TOTL.CD",
  start = 2015,
  end = 2024,
  extra = TRUE
)

reserves_wb <- reserves_api |>
  filter(region != "Aggregates") |>
  transmute(
    country,
    iso3c,
    year,
    reserves_million_usd = FI.RES.TOTL.CD / 1000000
  )


The table below compares six matched countries. The percentage difference is \(100 \times (Wikipedia - World\ Bank)/World\ Bank\). This is a comparison across vintages rather than an error rate. The World Bank value is from 2024, while the Wikipedia observations are mostly from 2026 and combine more recent reports from national sources. China, Japan, Switzerland, India, and Brazil have larger values in the newer Wikipedia observations, with gaps ranging from about 3.3% to 14.2%. The United States differs in the opposite direction by about 72.1%. The date gap may explain part of the differences, but it does not establish the cause. In particular, the U.S. result requires checking the definitions and original sources used by each provider before deciding that either value is incorrect.

title: Assignment 4: Web Scraping and Data Acquisition Plan
section: 4. Web data acquisition plan: Kerr County flood discourse on X
text:
4. Web data acquisition plan: Kerr County flood discourse on X

Source and purpose
My research asks: To whom, and on what grounds, is responsibility for flood warnings and response attributed in X discourse about the July 2025 Kerr County flood, and how are these claims rebutted? X is the appropriate primary source because the object of study is responsibility discourse on that platform. News articles or official warning archives can be used to check factual claims and reconstruct the warning timeline, but they cannot substitute for the posts being analyzed.
For the current project, I used the X full-archive search API to collect 8,294 English-language posts from July 4–6, 2025, using Texas local time. The search combined place names—Kerr County, Kerrville, Camp Mystic, and Guadalupe River—with flood terms and responsibility or actor terms, including warning, sirens, NWS, NOAA, FEMA, officials, Trump, and budget cuts. Retweets were excluded. After duplicate texts and one post containing webpage code were removed, 7,262 posts remained. The collection record will retain the complete query, endpoint, requested fields, time zone, collection date, and cleaning decisions.


Permission and method
I will use X’s authenticated API rather than scrape the public website. Because this method does not request X web pages, robots.txt does not govern the API calls. If a later stage requires any page request, I will check its exact path before the first request and will not proceed if it is disallowed. API use is governed by the current X Developer Agreement, Developer Policy, and the conditions of my access level. I will review them before another collection or release. Credentials will remain outside the script, and shared material will follow the applicable storage and redistribution rules. Full-archive search also provides structured fields, pagination, and a bounded historical query. Scraping search-result pages would be less reproducible and is unnecessary while authorized API access is available.


Volume, rate limits, and caching
During collection, I will monitor the endpoint’s rate-limit information. Each successful response page will be cached immediately in a restricted raw-data directory with its request time, query information, and pagination token. After a rate-limit error, the script will stop and resume after the indicated reset. The collection log will allow a restarted job to continue from the last completed page instead of downloading it again. Untouched responses will remain separate from the cleaned file. The log will record returned posts, duplicate removals, excluded retweets, failed requests, and the final number of records. Access tokens will not be written to the data or log.


Changes, detection, and limitations
Changes to response fields, pagination, endpoint access, rate limits, or search operators could break the collection. I will first run a small pilot and verify field names, data types, timestamp range, language values, unique identifiers, and pagination metadata. The script will stop if a required field is absent. Page-level counts and missing-value summaries will make unusual shifts visible, and the collection record will date the documentation and terms consulted.
The corpus is not a representative sample of public opinion. It is limited by the three-day period, English filter, search terms, excluded retweets, deletion or privacy changes, and the population using X. I will report these limits and will publish only the acquisition procedure and aggregate counts on the assignment website, not the raw post text.

title: Assignment 6: Text Analytics with quanteda
text:
I constructed three quanteda corpora: archived summit tweets, GovInfo presidential documents, and inaugural addresses. Their different production and selection processes determine what the results can mean.
The tweet archive contains 14,520 posts dated November 7–16, 2021, including 9,035 retweets (62.2%). Biden, Xi, summit, and virtual dominate the cleaned word counts. The hashtag network connects leader names with coronavirus, fentanyl, and human-rights tags. Mention clusters include journalists and NBA-related accounts. Edges represent co-occurrence within tweets, not direct communication. Retweets can amplify these patterns. Four-dimensional LSA separates vocabulary such as summit/virtual from old/friend, suggesting differences in coverage and framing rather than validated political positions.
Tweets were produced by platform users, including media and advocacy accounts, for their followers and wider audiences. The archive’s keyword selection and collection window make it a record of selected discourse, not representative public opinion. Its original API access cannot be reproduced today. The exact original collection query was not supplied with the script.
The CPD search returned 351 documents, all successfully downloaded: 183 assigned to Biden and 168 to Trump. KWIC shows Xi appearing in substantive discussion and editorial notes or name indexes. In one Biden passage, he describes having spent more time with Xi than other world leaders. Trump-associated keyness includes tariffs and great; Biden-associated words include national, security, and briefing. However, question labels such as q, editorial material, document genres, and unequal periods also influence this comparison. It does not isolate changes in China policy.
CPD materials originate from White House releases and are reviewed and annotated by Office of the Federal Register editors for an official public record. They reveal official presentation; tweets reveal selected circulation and reactions. The tweets concern the 2021 summit window, whereas CPD covers several years, so these are not equivalent samples of the summit or US–China relations.

title: Assignment 6: Text Analytics with quanteda
text:
Inaugural addresses
The corpus contains 21 addresses from 1945 through 2025; Trump’s 2025 address is already included. Length ranges from 555 tokens in Roosevelt’s 1945 address to 2,909 in Trump’s 2025 address. With a 100-token MATTR window, Reagan’s 1985 address has the highest lexical diversity (0.711), and Nixon’s 1973 address the lowest (0.640). Flesch–Kincaid grade estimates range from 5.78 for Biden to 12.30 for Nixon in 1973. These indicate textual properties, not intelligence or actual audience comprehension.
The most similar pair is Reagan’s 1981 and 1985 addresses (cosine 0.690); Reagan 1985 and Clinton 1997 also resemble each other (0.642). Republican-associated words include federal, government, and freedom; Democratic-associated words include democracy and change. Presidents, historical circumstances, and unequal speech lengths complicate party interpretations. Inaugurals are ceremonial statements addressed to the nation, selected by an institutional tradition rather than keyword searches.

title: Assignment 6: Text Analytics with quanteda
text:
What Wordfish measures
Wordfish assumes conditionally independent Poisson word counts, with log expected counts combining document and word effects and an interaction between document position and word discrimination. It estimates one latent dimension without assigning its substantive meaning. Here positions correlate with year (r = 0.847), and parties overlap considerably. Earlier-associated words include international and peoples; later-associated words include going and thank. This suggests historical vocabulary and rhetorical change, but validation would require close reading, external measures, and preprocessing checks. It is insufficient to label the axis liberal–conservative. I set dir using 1945 Roosevelt and 2025 Trump to fix the otherwise reversible axis orientation; this does not establish meaning.

title: Assignment 7: YouTube API and Election Comments
text:
On November 17, 2026, I collected YouTube metadata and comments using tuber 3.0.0 and an API key stored outside the script. I searched US midterm election with relevance and view-count ordering, requesting 100 results each for September 1–October 27 and November 4–collection time. The two orderings shared 16 unique videos before Election Day and 24 afterward. Al Jazeera English led the pre-election relevance results; CNN dominated both view-count lists. FRANCE 24 English led post-election relevance results. Each response reported 1,000,000 results but returned only 100 rows, including duplicates. The reported total is not a verified inventory.
I selected NBC News, CNN, and Al Jazeera English to compare a US broadcast network, cable news, and an international broadcaster. Their uploads required 81, 63, and 81 pages respectively to reach September 1. The channel route found election-related titles absent from the capped searches. My title filter was midterm|election|senate|house race|ballot. Reviewing 20 retained and 20 dropped titles revealed foreign-election false positives and likely omissions among generically titled programs. I excluded identified foreign-election patterns, but did not validate every retained video. From each channel and publication period, I selected the two videos with the most reported comments.
All 12 requests succeeded, returning 300 comments each: 3,600 total. Reported counts ranged from 659 to 21,040. The cap explains incomplete coverage; moderation, deletion, reply availability, and API ordering may also affect access, but these logs cannot quantify their individual effects. No selected video returned a disabled-comments status. This does not establish channel-wide moderation practices.

title: Assignment 7: YouTube API and Election Comments
text:
What the comments represent
The corpus unit is one comment, including replies, with channel, video, publication period, reply status, likes, and comment date as document variables. Comment IDs were deduplicated and connected to unique video metadata. A critical timing check found that 918 of 1,800 comments on pre-election videos were written on or after November 4. Thus, this is a retrospective comparison of video publication windows, not historical snapshots of opinion before and after voting.
Replies ranged from 0% to 28.2% across channel-period groups. Median likes were zero throughout. In CNN’s post-election group, the top 1% of comments received 60.6% of likes, and the most active 10% of identifiable authors produced 29.5% of comments. Repeated text beyond the first occurrence ranged from zero to 22 rows per group. These patterns show unequal participation and attention; repetition alone does not establish automation.

title: Assignment 7: YouTube API and Election Comments
text:
Text analysis and validation
Before modeling, I inspected 20 KWIC lines each for democrat*, republican*, trump, vote*, and ballot*. Party labels and candidate references frequently carried blame or ridicule; ballot language often figuratively linked Trump to the midterm result. Grievances about suppression or fraud are commenters’ assertions, not verified events. I lowercased tokens, removed URLs, mentions, punctuation and numbers, and retained emoji. English stopwords were removed for keyness. Five specified election phrases were compounded, alongside the observed phrases civil war and voter suppression.
Channel-versus-others keyness distinguished hearts, celebration and religious expressions for Al Jazeera English; Trump and other named figures for CNN; and polls, voting and wave emoji for NBC. Post-election-video comments emphasized Texas, civil war, voting and losing. These differences may reflect selected video subjects, formats and audiences rather than stable channel ideology.
LSD2015 dictionary scores were more positive for post-election videos on Al Jazeera English and CNN, with little change for NBC. However, my independent coding of 40 randomly sampled comments agreed with the dictionary on only 13 (32.5%). Human labels were 11 positive, 19 negative and 10 neither. Sarcasm, ridicule, mixed sentiment and implicit praise make dictionary results unreliable as substantive conclusions.

title: Assignment 7: YouTube API and Election Comments
text:
Comparison and data note
Assignment 6’s summit tweets reflect platform users selected by the archived collection, while presidential documents reflect institutional communication selected through official records. These YouTube comments reflect self-selected participants beneath particular news videos, further selected by popularity, API availability, ordering and caps. Tweets and comments support bounded claims about observed communication; presidential documents support claims about official presentation. None directly measures representative public opinion. Official records are generally easier to recollect; social-media results change with availability and platform access.
This collection used the YouTube Data API under its terms, with separate search and data budgets. Logs record eight search calls and 283 data units. Both publication-window manifests specify deletion by December 17, 2026; raw API data will be deleted within 30 days. Only logs, manifests, aggregate tables and plots accompany this report. API keys, raw comments and commenter identities are excluded.
